title: From The Trap Of Geopolitics To A Geo-Civilizational Paradigm | NOEMA
gist: Drawing on Bruno Maçães' Berggruen Press book 'In Search Of Greater India,' Gardels argues the nation-state is a Western export that traps rising powers like India and China in dualistic, escalation-prone geopolitics, and that only a 'geo-civilizational' frame rooted in Advaita nondualism offers an exit. He concedes the paradox that civilizational identity can only be asserted through the very modern state power that contradicts it, and closes pessimistically on the timeline: 'What has been a long time gone will be a long time coming.'

insights.claim: The nation-state is framed as a Western invention that leaves non-Western states structurally exposed to Western influence, while civilizations are positioned as the durable alternative unit of political identity.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Analysts modeling India, China or Gulf policy should price civilizational-identity drivers, not just national-interest calculus — it changes what these states treat as non-negotiable.
insights.quote: Nation-states are a Western invention, naturally vulnerable to Western influence. Civilizations are an alternative to the West
insights.locator: the Portuguese diplomat and scholar Bruno Maçães

insights.claim: Postcolonial states inherited the institutional mold of the Western imperialism they replaced, and only began reclaiming civilizational roots once they grew strong and prosperous enough to stand alone — making civilizational assertion a function of accumulated national power.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Implies civilizational assertiveness scales with GDP and capability, so expect more of it from India and China, not less, as their economies compound.
insights.quote: Only as they became strong and prosperous enough to stand on their own did the likes of China and India break free from that shadow of history and reclaim their civilizational roots

insights.claim: There is a self-undermining paradox in civilizational politics: the only vehicle capable of asserting a civilization's foundational identity is the modern state inside an international order whose interests contradict that civilization's holistic outlook.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: A structural reason to discount rhetoric about civilizational harmony from rising powers — the delivery mechanism guarantees conventional realpolitik behavior.
insights.quote: the wherewithal for asserting their foundational identity only resides within the power of modern states situated in an international order, the interests of which are at odds with the holism of their civilizational outlook.

themes.theme: Psychology of national ego and escalation

insights.claim: Applying Carl Jung's account of the insecure ego to states, the argument is that nations project their repressed traits onto rivals, manufacturing the very monsters they then feel compelled to destroy — a self-generating mechanism for good-versus-evil conflict framing.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: A model for reading escalation cycles as endogenous rather than event-driven: rival demonization tends to intensify regardless of the adversary's actual conduct.
insights.quote: The monsters we confront are the monsters we ourselves have created. And since they are all too ready to destroy us, we must be ready to destroy them.
insights.locator: He cites Carl Jung on the unenlightened

insights.claim: Demand for international rules and order is described as spiking precisely when actors feel most vulnerable as egos in political conflict — order is a symptom of insecurity, not of confidence.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Predicts that calls for new global governance architecture will cluster around crisis peaks and fade in calm periods — treat rules-based-order rhetoric as a fear indicator.
insights.quote: It is precisely when we feel most vulnerable as an ego subject to the conflicts of the political world that we call for rules and order, concepts that can exist only on a higher plane.
insights.locator: Indian philosophy, according to Maçães, teaches

insights.claim: Durable world order is claimed to be impossible to build on power itself, and can only grow from a deliberate detachment from power — an explicit rejection of realist balance-of-power foundations.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Directly contradicts the operating assumption of most defense and geopolitical risk models; useful as a stress-test of consensus multipolarity narratives, not as a base case.
insights.quote: World order can never be based on power but must grow from the effort to detach ourselves from power and from the world, having experienced its joys but knowing its limits.
insights.locator: Even when conflict resorts to force

themes.theme: Advaita nondualism as political operating system

insights.claim: Advaita nondualism is offered as a reusable political framework in which ego-versus-other opposition is treated as the lowest level of consciousness and personal identity as a temporary mask, dissolving the in-group/out-group logic that underpins nationalism.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: The intellectual scaffolding behind India's 'civilizational state' soft-power pitch — expect it to surface in Indian diplomatic framing and Global South positioning.
insights.quote: In Indian thought, dualism has been repeatedly rebutted. Advaita, or nondualism, sees the opposition between ego and other as proper to the lowest level of consciousness

insights.claim: Shashi Tharoor's formulation that in Christianity the body has a soul while in Hinduism the soul has a body is used to argue that ethical obligation to others is self-interest rather than altruism, making Western moral theory look 'churlish' by comparison.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Shows how senior Indian officials package religious philosophy as exportable moral doctrine — a soft-power vector distinct from economic or military statecraft.
insights.quote: whereas in Christianity the body has a soul, in Hinduism the soul has a body. In other words, we are emanations of a universal soul, the atman.

insights.claim: Arnold Toynbee is invoked for the binary claim that a historical chapter with a Western beginning must have an Indian ending — 'either the Indian way or the bomb' — framing nondualism and nuclear catastrophe as the only two terminal states.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: A framing device for tail-risk thinking: the essay's own logic gives no middle path between civilizational reconciliation and nuclear use.
insights.quote: It will be either the ‘Indian way’ or the bomb.
insights.locator: It is from within this perspective that he cites

insights.claim: India tested its first nuclear device in 1974 under the name 'Smiling Buddha,' nearly 30 years after independence, and tested again in 1998 as 'Operation Shakti' — evidence that Advaita's civilizational light did not restrain the Indian nation-state's weaponization.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: The concrete counterexample to the essay's own thesis: philosophical tradition has zero observed restraining power on hard-security decisions, so don't underweight escalation risk on cultural grounds.
insights.quote: the Indian nation-state nevertheless tested its first nuclear device in 1974 (named “Smiling Buddha”), nearly 30 years after independence

insights.claim: Benazir Bhutto, then Pakistan's opposition leader, publicly called for a preemptive strike to destroy India's nuclear capacity in a column for Gardels' Global Viewpoint syndication network after India's 1998 test, and Pakistan conducted its own first nuclear test later that same year — making it the only Muslim-majority nuclear state.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: A documented case of mimetic nuclear escalation running from public rhetoric to a test within months — a template for how fast proliferation cascades can move.
insights.quote: Pakistan’s then-opposition leader Benazir Bhutto hotheadedly called in a column for my Global Viewpoint syndication network for a preemptive strike against her neighbor to destroy its nuclear capacity.
insights.locator: When India conducted its next test in 1998

themes.theme: Colonized minds and the civilizational-power trap

insights.claim: Peter Sloterdijk argues the Eastern mind has been colonized by the instrumental reason of the Western Enlightenment, so Daoist alignment with the natural order became newly plausible for the climate age at exactly the moment it was lost in China where it originated.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Cuts against the hope that Chinese tradition supplies a native brake on extractive growth — expect Chinese climate policy to stay instrumentalist and industrial-policy-driven.
insights.quote: Paradoxically, at the very moment the truth of the old Asian worldview shows its plausibility anew, it has been lost where it originated.

insights.claim: Wang Gungwu's test is that civilizations can coexist across boundaries safely, and danger arises specifically when 'civilization power' is claimed as universal and conflated with national interests.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: A usable screening signal: watch for states fusing universalist civilizational claims with national interest — that conflation, not civilizational diversity itself, marks rising conflict risk.
insights.quote: civilizations can coexist across boundaries, but when ‘civilization power’ is claimed as universal and conflated with national interests, the world becomes a dangerous place.
insights.locator: As the Chinese-Singaporean historian Wang Gungwu

insights.claim: Geopolitics inside an international order is characterized as a trap that inexorably invites conflict because dualistic mentality is constitutive of the order itself, with a geo-civilizational paradigm presented as the only exit — but one the author expects to take a very long time.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Even the essay's advocate treats the alternative as generational, so the practical base case remains structurally conflict-prone geopolitics for the investable horizon.
insights.quote: What has been a long time gone will be a long time coming.
insights.locator: The trap of geopolitics in an international order
